title: AnomSeer: Reasoning over Time Series
one_liner: Teach a vision-language model to explain what is normal and abnormal in time-series data by grounding its thinking in precise statistical details.
lead: Multimodal large language models (models trained to read images and text at the same time) can answer questions about pictures, but they struggle when you ask them to find unusual patterns in charts or sensor readings. AnomSeer addresses this by forcing the model to base its explanations on precise mathematical measures—like how spread-out the numbers are, or what frequencies show up in the data—rather than loose, vague descriptions.

problem.h2: Vision-language models see the picture but miss the numbers
paras: A chart shows temperature readings from a factory sensor over a month. Most days the line bounces between 70 and 75 degrees. Then one day it shoots up to 95. A model trained to describe images can see there is a spike, but it cannot easily say whether 95 is actually abnormal or just normal noise—it has to guess based on patterns it memorized, without doing real math. When the data has multiple dimensions (five sensors at once, or a weekly pattern buried in daily noise), this guesswork fails completely.

A human engineer, by contrast, would compute how far 95 sits from the average, check whether it violates the normal frequency spectrum, and then write down exactly what makes it anomalous, because doing math anchors the verdict to measurable facts rather than guesses. The model needs to learn to do that work too, not just eyeball the chart.

callout.b: The paper's core move in one sentence.
callout.html: AnomSeer trains the model to always justify its anomaly verdict by computing and naming precise statistics—like mean, variance, and dominant frequencies—before declaring something abnormal.

steps.text: A human engineer analyzes each anomaly by hand, computing mean, standard deviation, frequency content. This trace becomes ground truth.
The model reads the chart and the expert trace together, learning to output similar step-by-step explanations with real numbers.

steps.b: Step 3: Reward signal from transport distance
steps.text: A mathematical measure (optimal transport) grades how well the model's statistical explanation matches the expert one.
The model gets nudged to match the reward (reinforcement learning), but an orthogonal projection ensures the granular reward does not accidentally break the main detection accuracy.
The model outputs both a yes/no anomaly verdict and a chain of reasoning anchored in precise statistics.

paras: The paper changes what the model outputs. Instead of just saying 'this is anomalous' or 'this is normal', it now must produce a step-by-step written reasoning that includes computed statistics before the final label. This turns a black-box guess into a transparent chain of thought.

hidden.name: quality of the reasoning chain
paras: A reasoning chain's quality is how closely it matches an expert's chain. An expert has computed the mean, the deviation from mean, maybe the frequency spectrum. If the model outputs similar statements with similar numbers, the expert and model are aligned. If the model makes up numbers or skips steps, they drift apart.

The paper estimates this alignment using optimal transport—a mathematical measure of how much 'cost' it would take to warp one statistical description into the other. Smaller cost means the model's reasoning is closer to the expert's reasoning.

heat.caption: Darker means more critical to the reasoning trace. Highlighted cells anchor the model to verifiable details.

reads.html: The model's explanation is good if it names the same measurements an expert would, in roughly the same order, with numbers in the same ballpark.

Optimal transport computes the Wasserstein distance between expert and model statistical descriptions, scoring alignment. Orthogonal projection ensures this auxiliary signal preserves the main detection objective.

mechanism.h2: Why grounding in statistics makes the model reason better
paras: When a model is trained only to say yes/no, it can hide whatever it wants inside its hidden layers—it might learn a shortcut that looks good on test data but breaks on new data. When you force it to spell out its math first, you create a bottleneck: it must compute statistics, and those numbers either match reality or they do not. If the model says 'mean is 73' and the actual mean is 50, the expert will catch it immediately.

The reinforcement learning part (reward based on transport distance) pushes the model toward expert-style reasoning, but reinforcement learning has its own pitfall: over-optimizing for the reward signal can degrade the main task (finding anomalies correctly). The paper's solution is orthogonal projection—a geometric trick that splits the push-toward-better-reasoning from the push-toward-better-detection, because when two objectives compete, forcing them to remain perpendicular ensures neither can steal resources from the other. This prevents the reward for good explanations from accidentally breaking the detector.

stages.s: Compute statistics: mean, variance, frequency spectrum
Output chain-of-thought: 'mean is X, deviation is Y, frequency shows Z'
Compare to expert chain via optimal transport; apply orthogonal projection

math.h2: The grounding formula and worked example
math.words: The reward for good reasoning is the negative transport distance from the model's statistics to the expert's statistics, scaled by a factor. The total training loss combines the anomaly detection loss and this grounded reward, separated by orthogonal projection so they do not interfere.
symbols: how wrong the anomaly verdict is (classification or localization error)
the combined training loss to minimize
the strength of the grounding reward
optimal transport distance (Wasserstein) between two statistical descriptions
the statistics the human expert computed
orthogonal projection that removes any component pointing toward the detection loss gradient

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Sensor reads: [72, 73, 72, 74, 95]. Expert says: mean=73.2, std=8.9, threshold=90.
Model says: mean=72, std=9, threshold=90. Transport distance between (73.2,8.9) and (72,9) is 1.5.
Grounding reward = 0.1 * (-1.5) = -0.15 (smaller distance = bigger reward, so negative distance is positive reward).
Detection loss for the 95 verdict = 0.2. Total loss = 0.2 - 0.15 = 0.05 (the grounding helped reduce it).
Without projection, pushing to minimize loss might break detection accuracy; projection keeps the two objectives aligned.

math.note: The model learns to output statistics that match an expert's, without sacrificing its core job of correctly spotting anomalies.

charts.title: Naive multimodal model
charts.note: A model trained only on yes/no produces vague answers and cannot explain its work.

charts.title: AnomSeer with grounding
charts.note: Grounding in expert reasoning chains improves both detection and explanation quality, because when the model must output step-by-step math it exposes any errors in its logic and forces it to stay consistent with what the data actually shows.

items.html: If the human engineer who traces the ground truth makes a systematic error, the model will learn it. The method is only as good as the expert traces it copies.

items.b: The transport distance metric misses important dimensions.
items.html: Optimal transport measures closeness between sets of statistics. If the true reason for an anomaly is something the statistics do not capture (e.g., a rare event that has no historical precedent), the grounding reward will be blind to it.

items.b: Orthogonal projection is imperfect in high dimensions.
items.html: Orthogonal projection works well when the detection and grounding signals are nearly uncorrelated. If the model absolutely cannot do both simultaneously (a hard trade-off), the projection may not resolve it cleanly.

items.b: Done right: careful validation of expert traces and testing on unseen anomalies.
items.html: Before training, audit the expert's reasoning. After training, validate the model on held-out anomalies that the expert did not see, to ensure the model learned to reason, not merely copy.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small time-series dataset with known anomalies—e.g., five temperature sensors over one month, with three manually-injected anomalies (a spike, a persistent shift, a frequency corruption). Train AnomSeer on half, validate on the other half. Collect two kinds of output: (1) the final anomaly verdict (yes/no), and (2) the reasoning chain (mean, standard deviation, frequency observed, threshold crossed). Compare the model's reasoning to a human's reasoning on the same data.
demo.metric_eq: accuracy = (correct verdicts) / (total verdicts); reasoning alignment = transport distance between model chain and expert chain
demo.closing: The demo succeeds when the model's reasoning closely mirrors the expert's reasoning, not just because it guesses right, but because it computed the same statistics.
